edition: Chronicle Teaching Atlas · researched political lifecycles · 2026-09-27
scope: Selected sourced political lifecycles and explicitly bounded historical phases. Narratives do not validate border geometry; the separate state-coverage index describes every admitted source label and tracks remaining research gaps.

profiles.title: Early Dynastic Egypt
profiles.summary: Upper and Lower Egypt were gradually united under kings whose authority expanded during the first two dynasties. Memphis linked the two regions, while Abydos retained royal burial and ceremonial importance. These institutions developed into the more monumental kingship of the Old Kingdom.
profiles.continuity: This is an early phase of Egyptian kingship, not the lifetime of the modern state. Period boundaries vary between chronologies.

profiles.title: Old Kingdom Egypt
profiles.summary: The Old Kingdom developed the institutions and royal funerary traditions of the preceding dynasties. Pyramid construction and a powerful court mobilized resources on a large scale. Provincial elites became increasingly influential, and central rule fragmented as local governors gained autonomy.
profiles.continuity: The Ministry’s chronology is used here; other chronologies differ. Decentralization was a process, not a single national border change.

profiles.title: Middle Kingdom Egypt
profiles.summary: Mentuhotep II reunited Egypt after regional division. The kings of the Middle Kingdom renewed royal institutions, cultivated regional relationships, and sponsored major artistic and literary traditions. Political cohesion later weakened, giving way to the divided authority of the Second Intermediate Period.
profiles.continuity: Theban reunification and later royal residences belong to different phases; one permanent capital must not be projected across the entire period.

profiles.title: New Kingdom Egypt
profiles.summary: Ahmose I’s defeat of the Hyksos inaugurated a reunited kingdom. Eighteenth- through Twentieth-Dynasty rulers expanded into Nubia and western Asia and supported powerful temples, while royal religious policies and residences changed. Territorial losses and divided royal and priestly authority accompanied the end of the New Kingdom.
profiles.continuity: Thebes, Amarna, Memphis and the Ramesside Delta served different functions and periods. They are not interchangeable capitals.

profiles.title: Ptolemaic Kingdom
profiles.summary: After Alexander’s death, Ptolemy took control of Egypt and his dynasty developed a kingdom centered on Alexandria. Greek institutions coexisted with Egyptian kingship and temples, while the court supported scholarship and Mediterranean trade. Defeat by Octavian ended the dynasty and brought Egypt under Roman rule.
profiles.continuity: The opening date marks Ptolemy’s governorship, not his later assumption of the royal title. Roman conquest did not erase Egyptian or Greek communities.

profiles.title: Roman Republic
profiles.summary: Rome’s republican government developed after the traditional expulsion of its kings. Magistrates, the Senate and assemblies governed a state that expanded through Italy and across the Mediterranean. Competition over wealth, commands and citizenship helped generate civil wars, ending in Augustus’s dominant imperial position.
profiles.continuity: 509 BCE is a traditional foundation date. The transition to imperial rule retained republican offices rather than replacing every institution at once.

profiles.title: Roman Empire
profiles.periodLabel: 27 BCE–395 CE · before permanent court division
profiles.summary: Augustus consolidated power after republican civil wars. Imperial rule connected Mediterranean provinces through cities, armies and administration. Later crises encouraged shared rule; Constantine reunited the empire and founded Constantinople. After Theodosius I, separate eastern and western courts endured.
profiles.continuity: This profile follows the undivided imperial tradition, not all Roman civilization. Rome remained important after emperors established other residences.

profiles.title: Western Roman Empire
profiles.summary: The western court emerged from the division after Theodosius I. Provincial losses and competing military powers reduced its resources. Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476, conventionally marking the end of the western emperorship in Italy.
profiles.continuity: Roman institutions and communities continued under successor rulers; 476 is not the end of Roman life.

profiles.title: Eastern Roman / Byzantine Empire
profiles.summary: Centered on Constantinople, the eastern Roman state developed into a Christian, predominantly Greek-speaking empire whose people still called themselves Romans. Expansion and contraction reshaped its provinces. The Fourth Crusade shattered the imperial center in 1204; a restored court returned in 1261. Ottoman conquest ended that court in 1453.
profiles.continuity: Byzantine is a later historical label. Constantinople was under Latin rule in 1204–1261, while competing Roman successor courts survived elsewhere.

profiles.title: Achaemenid Empire
profiles.summary: Cyrus’s defeat of the Median king began a rapidly expanding Persian empire. His successors governed diverse regions through satraps, roads and several royal centers. The monarchy survived revolts and dynastic conflicts until Alexander’s campaigns and the death of Darius III ended Achaemenid rule.
profiles.continuity: Persepolis was a dynastic center alongside other royal seats; a single modern-style capital is misleading. Conquest unfolded region by region.

profiles.title: Seleucid Kingdom
profiles.summary: Seleucus built a successor kingdom out of Alexander’s contested conquests. Its rulers founded cities and connected Syria, Mesopotamia and Iranian lands, while fighting other Hellenistic monarchies. Territorial losses to Rome, Parthia and regional rulers reduced it to a Syrian kingdom, which Rome annexed.
profiles.continuity: 312 BCE follows the Seleucid era convention. Control was never uniform, and declining extent must not be inferred from the dynasty’s continuing name.

profiles.title: Parthian Empire
profiles.summary: The Arsacid rulers rose in northeastern Iran as Seleucid authority weakened. They expanded into Iran and Mesopotamia, combining royal power with strong regional elites and making Ctesiphon an important residence. Rivalry with Rome continued until Ardashir’s forces displaced the Arsacid monarchy.
profiles.continuity: The empire used multiple royal centers. The conventional dynastic beginning does not mean its later territory was already controlled in 247 BCE.

profiles.title: Sasanian Empire
profiles.summary: Ardashir I overthrew Parthian rule and established a new Persian dynasty. Sasanian rulers strengthened kingship, patronized Zoroastrian institutions and contested borderlands with Rome and eastern powers. Prolonged warfare and internal conflict preceded the Arab conquests; the last king, Yazdgard III, died in 651.
profiles.continuity: The dynasty’s end followed a sequence of territorial losses. Persian languages, institutions and communities continued after the monarchy fell.

profiles.title: Umayyad Caliphate
profiles.summary: Muawiya established dynastic caliphal rule after the first Islamic civil war. Damascus became the center of an empire extending from the Atlantic region to the Indus, with Arabic administration and new religious monuments. The Abbasid revolution displaced this dynasty in the central and eastern Islamic lands.
profiles.continuity: The later Umayyad polity in Iberia was a distinct continuation, not the unchanged Damascus caliphate.

profiles.title: Abbasid Caliphate
profiles.summary: The Abbasids replaced the Umayyads and established Baghdad, later ruling for a period from Samarra. Their courts supported commerce, scholarship and the arts. Regional dynasties gradually took effective power while caliphs retained religious authority. The Mongol capture of Baghdad ended the Iraqi caliphate.
profiles.continuity: Capital chronology includes the Samarra interval. Later nominal Abbasid caliphs in Egypt are not territorial continuation of the Baghdad empire.

profiles.title: Ottoman Empire
profiles.summary: An Anatolian frontier principality became a dynasty ruling across southeastern Europe, western Asia and North Africa. Constantinople became its imperial center after conquest. Government and provincial relationships changed over centuries, while later wars and territorial losses transformed the empire. Ottoman sultanic rule ended in 1922.
profiles.continuity: 1299 is a conventional founding date. The empire did not become a single successor country: many territories followed different political paths.

profiles.title: Safavid Iran
profiles.summary: The Safavids united Iran under a dynasty that promoted Twelver Shiism. Royal patronage, trade and administrative reform supported successive courts at Tabriz, Qazvin and Isfahan. Afghan conquest broke the imperial center in 1722; restoration under military patrons did not restore the earlier monarchy’s independence.
profiles.continuity: 1722 marks collapse of effective rule; 1736 marks the dynasty’s replacement by Nader Shah. These different endpoints should not be collapsed.

profiles.title: Mughal Empire
profiles.periodLabel: 1526–1858 CE · interrupted rule, then nominal survival
profiles.summary: Babur’s conquests founded the Mughal dynasty; after Humayun’s exile, Akbar consolidated a major South Asian empire. Successors sponsored rich court cultures and cities, but provincial power and external conquests eroded central authority. By the nineteenth century the emperors were largely nominal; British rule removed the last emperor.
profiles.continuity: The Sur interregnum interrupted Mughal control in northern India. Court survival after territorial fragmentation does not imply continued control of the former empire.

profiles.title: Mauryan Empire
profiles.summary: Chandragupta Maurya united a large realm from a northeastern South Asian base at Pataliputra. Bindusara and Ashoka extended imperial authority, while Ashoka’s inscriptions and religious patronage left unusually direct evidence of kingship. The dynasty ended in the second century BCE and its territories passed to regional successor powers.
profiles.continuity: The beginning varies by chronology; the museum title uses c. 323 BCE and its narrative c. 321 BCE. Territorial control changed throughout the dynasty.

profiles.title: Han dynasty
profiles.periodLabel: 206 BCE–220 CE · Western and Eastern Han
profiles.summary: The Han reunited China after the Qin collapse and civil war. Western Han government centered on Chang’an; after an interruption, Eastern Han ruled from Luoyang. Imperial institutions, territorial expansion and long-distance exchange shaped the era. The dynasty’s collapse opened a prolonged period of competing states.
profiles.continuity: Western and Eastern Han were separated by Wang Mang’s Xin regime and the restoration struggles; the entire span is not continuous Han rule.

profiles.title: Tang dynasty
profiles.summary: The Tang followed the Sui and developed a powerful imperial state. Chang’an and Luoyang were major capitals linked to wide diplomatic and commercial networks. Court culture drew on exchanges across Asia. The dynasty ended in 907, followed by competing dynasties and regional kingdoms.
profiles.continuity: Tang rule was interrupted by Wu Zetian’s Zhou dynasty. Two capital cities and a mobile court make a single fixed seat misleading.

profiles.title: Song dynasty
profiles.summary: The Song dynasty emerged from post-Tang division and developed a prosperous commercial and administrative state. The loss of northern territory forced the court from Kaifeng to the south, where Hangzhou became its center. Southern Song endured until Mongol conquest completed the Yuan takeover.
profiles.continuity: Northern and Southern Song denote phases of one dynasty, with a profound territorial and capital break. Its neighbors were independent powers.

profiles.continuity: The Yuan was part of the divided Mongol world. Northern Yuan continuations after 1368 are outside this profile’s Chinese imperial scope.

profiles.title: Ming dynasty
profiles.summary: Zhu Yuanzhang founded the Ming after the collapse of Yuan rule and made Nanjing his capital. The main court later moved to Beijing. Commercial expansion and cultural production accompanied almost three centuries of rule, before rebellion and Manchu conquest brought down the principal court.
profiles.continuity: Southern Ming claimants continued after Beijing fell. Nanjing retained a secondary-capital role after the northern move; modern city names alone do not encode those distinctions.

profiles.title: Qing dynasty
profiles.summary: Manchu rulers captured Beijing and built a multiethnic empire using both inherited Chinese institutions and their own traditions. Eighteenth-century expansion and prosperity were followed by wars, unequal treaties and internal rebellions. The 1911 revolution and the emperor’s abdication in 1912 ended imperial rule.
profiles.continuity: 1644 begins this profile’s Beijing-centered phase, not the dynasty’s earlier formation in Manchuria. Modern China is a separate political identity.

profiles.title: Mali Empire
profiles.summary: Mande chiefdoms united under Sunjata to create Mali’s imperial power. Gold trade and far-reaching political connections supported its expansion, while Mansa Musa’s pilgrimage made the court famous abroad. Regional rivals and shifting power gradually reduced the empire; its fragmentation did not end Mande political traditions.
profiles.continuity: The beginning and end are approximate. Its court’s location and political geography remain debated; this is distinct from the modern Republic of Mali.

profiles.title: Songhai Empire
profiles.summary: The state centered on Gao expanded under Sunni Ali and the Askia rulers, connecting Niger trade cities and regional territories. Muslim scholarship flourished alongside varied local traditions. Moroccan forces defeated the imperial army in 1591 and occupied major cities, while resistance continued outside them.
profiles.continuity: Earlier Gao and later Songhai successor communities are not the same territorial empire. Defeat did not make the population or its traditions disappear.

profiles.title: Kingdom of Benin
profiles.periodLabel: c. 1200–1897 CE · dynasty and independent kingdom
profiles.summary: The royal dynasty at Benin developed from older Edo political traditions. Its court became a major political, religious and artistic center, commissioning works from specialist guilds. British forces captured and looted Benin City in 1897 and exiled the oba, ending the kingdom’s independent rule.
profiles.continuity: The Edo kingdom lay in present-day Nigeria, not the modern country named Benin. Royal and cultural continuity survived colonial conquest.

profiles.title: Zimbabwe state at Great Zimbabwe
profiles.periodLabel: c. 12th–15th centuries · principal period of influence
profiles.summary: A regional state grew around Great Zimbabwe’s stone-built urban center. Farming, cattle, metalworking and exchange with the Indian Ocean supported its influence across the plateau. Its political prominence declined in the later fifteenth century as Khami grew, although occupation and sacred connections continued.
profiles.continuity: These bounds describe the principal state-building period, not settlement birth and death. Archaeology places occupation across the eleventh through seventeenth centuries.

profiles.title: Mexica Triple Alliance
profiles.summary: Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan formed an alliance after defeating Azcapotzalco. Expansion built a tributary and political network across central Mexico, with Tenochtitlan increasingly dominant. The conquest of Tenochtitlan ended the imperial alliance in 1521, while Indigenous communities and institutions continued under colonial rule.
profiles.continuity: This was an alliance with several political centers, not a uniformly administered modern nation-state. Mexica and allied peoples did not disappear with conquest.

profiles.title: Inka Empire / Tawantinsuyu

Growth transformed a regional kingdom into a vast empire within a century. Spanish invasion broke the main imperial center, although resistance and Inka political and cultural traditions continued.

Monumental avenues, temples and diverse neighborhoods supported wide commercial and cultural connections. Conflict and the destruction of important buildings accompanied political decline; smaller communities continued after the city lost its earlier authority.

profiles.title: Monte Albán state
profiles.summary: Established on a hill overlooking the Oaxaca valleys, Monte Albán developed into a major political and ceremonial capital. Its rulers organized tribute and monumental building, while elite tombs reveal pronounced social distinctions. Regional authority eventually fragmented and the capital’s political role ended, although its buildings and sacred landscape retained later importance.
profiles.continuity: The end of capital status is placed around 800–850 CE. This broad endpoint does not mean that all inhabitants or regional communities disappeared.

profiles.title: Chile
profiles.summary: Independence was declared in 1818 after a struggle interrupted by Spanish reconquest. Republican institutions developed through constitutional conflict, economic change and territorial expansion. Civil war transformed the political system in 1891. The 1973 military coup began a dictatorship; elected civilian government returned in 1990. The state continues today.
profiles.continuity: Regime changes and territorial changes have separate chronologies. The 2025 lookup limit is the atlas’s coverage endpoint, not the end of Chile.

profiles.title: Mamluk Sultanate
profiles.summary: Military elites of slave-soldier origin replaced Ayyubid rule in Egypt and expanded into Syria. Cairo linked Mediterranean and Indian Ocean commerce; sultans and emirs endowed mosques, schools, hospitals and markets. Recruitment into a military household mattered alongside descent. Plague, factional struggles and changing trade affected the realm before Ottoman conquest in 1517.
profiles.continuity: Bahri and Burji are period labels within changing elite networks. Authority over provincial governors and the holy cities differed from direct administration in the Egyptian core; a single fill cannot show these relationships.

profiles.title: Timurid realms
profiles.summary: Timur established power in Transoxiana and used Samarkand as the center of far-reaching conquests. After his death, dynastic branches competed for territories; later courts at Herat and Samarkand sustained Persian literary, artistic and architectural patronage. The western conquests were difficult to retain, and successor states displaced the remaining Timurid realms by the early sixteenth century.
profiles.continuity: An army’s campaign reach was not uniform civil administration. This profile follows a dynastic tradition whose realms divided; it does not imply one continuous border or a single capital.

profiles.title: Polish–Lithuanian dynastic union

Their association developed through negotiation rather than a single merger. The Union of Lublin later established a commonwealth of the two polities, building a new constitutional relationship on this longer history.

profiles.title: Golden Horde / Jochid realms
profiles.periodLabel: 13th century–1502 CE · Jochid formation and fragmentation
profiles.summary: Batu’s conquests established Jochid power in the western steppe; an autonomous khanate emerged in the 1260s. Successor khanates emerged before the Great Horde remnant’s defeat in 1502.
profiles.continuity: 1236 marks the conquest phase, not an uncontested foundation date. 1502 is a conventional endpoint for the Great Horde remnant; Jochid successor states and traditions continued. profiles.title: Hittite kingdom and empire

Royal centers changed, and the collapse of Hattusha around 1200 BCE ended the imperial structure while related traditions persisted in northern Syria.
profiles.continuity: The start follows the establishment of Hattusha as capital, not the first appearance of Hittite speakers. Subject kingdoms, royal domains and contested frontiers were different forms of authority.

Ashur remained a religious center while rulers built other capitals. Warfare at the end of the seventh century BCE destroyed the imperial political order.
profiles.continuity: This study covers the Middle and Neo-Assyrian periods, not all Assyrian history or the later identity of Assyrian communities. Provincial administration and tributary kingship should be distinguished.

profiles.title: Kush · Napatan and Meroitic periods
profiles.summary: Kushite power developed along the middle Nile with royal and sacred centers at Napata and Meroë. profiles.continuity: This profile covers the second kingdom of Kush, not earlier Kerma. Period boundaries are archaeological conventions, not exact dates of city disappearance or population replacement.

profiles.title: Aksumite kingdom
profiles.summary: Aksum linked the Ethiopian highlands with Red Sea commerce through Adulis and inland African exchange routes. Monumental stelae, royal tombs and multilingual inscriptions attest to its rulers and international connections. Christianity became important in the fourth century. Political power declined while Aksum retained ceremonial and religious significance.

profiles.title: Gupta Empire
profiles.summary: The Guptas rose in the Ganges region and expanded through conquest and marriage alliances. Some defeated rulers remained in place as tributaries. Royal patronage supported literature, religious institutions and art with influence far beyond the empire. Huna attacks and the loss of subordinate territories accompanied a contraction of power; the dynasty dissolved by the mid-sixth century.
profiles.continuity: The meaning of 320 CE as an accession or independence date is uncertain. The empire’s political reach was not uniform direct control, and its cultural influence outlasted the dynasty.

profiles.title: Qin state and empire
profiles.periodLabel: c. ninth century–206 BCE; empire 221–206 BCE
profiles.summary: Qin grew from a small Zhou fief in northwestern China into a military and administrative power. Its emergence belongs to the ninth century BCE; the opening date here is an approximate period marker. Fourth-century reforms associated with Shang Yang strengthened agricultural resources, military service and centralized government. Qin then conquered its rival states, and Ying Zheng adopted the imperial title in 221 BCE. Imperial officials administered commanderies and counties, while standardization of writing, measures and currency supported integration. Roads, canals, frontier construction and the emperor’s mausoleum also demanded extensive labour. The imperial dynasty was brief: after the First Emperor’s death in 210 BCE, its authority collapsed, and Han rule followed in 206 BCE. Several administrative practices outlived the ruling house.
profiles.continuity: The atlas labels Qin at 323 and 300 BCE describe the pre-imperial state. They must not inherit the full territory or institutions of the later unified empire. A dynasty’s fall is not the disappearance of its population or administrative traditions.

profiles.title: Jin dynasty · Western and Eastern
profiles.summary: The Sima imperial house established the Jin dynasty after the Three Kingdoms period. Its Western Jin phase briefly restored a wider imperial framework, but internal conflict and pressure from northern powers undermined that settlement. The destruction of the northern court’s position led members of the ruling house and other elites to the lower Yangzi. From 317, the Eastern Jin governed from Jiankang, at present-day Nanjing, while separate kingdoms controlled the north. Political division did not halt cultural production: calligraphy, painting and literature became enduring features of southern elite life. The Eastern Jin ended in 420 as another southern dynasty replaced it. This sequence combines a dynastic claim to continuity with a major contraction and relocation of government.
profiles.continuity: This Jin is the Sima dynasty of the third–fifth centuries, not the later Jurchen Jin. The 317 change marks a new political and geographic phase; one continuous colour must not imply that the earlier empire remained intact.

profiles.title: Northern Wei / Tuoba Wei
profiles.summary: Northern Wei was founded by the Tuoba ruling group of the Xianbei in the divided political world of northern China. Its rulers combined conquest and imperial institutions with patronage of Buddhism. Monumental cave temples at Yungang, near the northern capital of Pingcheng, expressed both religious devotion and royal authority. Emperor Xiaowen’s reforms encouraged Chinese court customs, surnames, dress and institutions; the move to Luoyang in 494 made that transformation especially visible. Connections across political boundaries carried artistic and religious practices between northern and southern courts. These changes also created tensions within the state. The Northern Wei dynastic framework broke apart in the mid-sixth century, followed by separate eastern and western governments. The surviving sculptures and inscriptions document particular patrons and communities, rather than the religious beliefs of every inhabitant.
profiles.continuity: The source spelling Toba Wei is matched only to Northern Wei’s dated span. Its Buddhist monuments do not establish a uniformly Buddhist population, and its political territory is distinct from the later Eastern Wei and Western Wei successor regimes.

profiles.title: Western Xia / Xixia
profiles.summary: The Tangut rulers established the Xixia imperial dynasty in 1038 in the region of present-day Ningxia and the corridors of northwestern China. Its position beside major overland routes brought the court into contact with caravans, monks and neighbouring peoples. Imperial institutions drew on Chinese models, while Tangut language, writing and traditions retained a distinctive place. Buddhism was prominent, alongside ancestral practices. The imperial cemetery below the Helan Mountains preserves a hierarchy of royal and subordinate tombs, buildings and flood-control works. These remains reveal an organized court and a society shaped by multiple cultural contacts. Mongol conquest destroyed the dynasty in 1227. The archaeological record preserves aspects of its religious and political organization, but does not turn every disputed frontier into an exact boundary.

profiles.title: Kushan imperial realms
profiles.summary: Kushan power developed from a branch of the Yuezhi groups that had moved into Bactria, then extended into Afghanistan and northwestern South Asia. The rulers connected inland caravan routes with networks reaching Arabian Sea ports. Their courts and cities supported trade and a varied religious life, reflected in coins, sculpture and inscriptions drawing on several traditions. Kanishka’s era was especially important for Buddhist patronage and artistic production in Gandhara and Mathura. The date of his accession remains debated, so a museum-dated coin around 130 CE is used as an evidential anchor rather than a precise reign boundary. In the third century, Sasanian expansion placed parts of the former imperial territory under new rulers known as Kushanshahs. Other Kushan lineages and institutions survived unevenly.
profiles.continuity: The first–third-century range is a broad imperial phase, not a settled foundation-to-extinction chronology. Yuezhi migration predates it; Kushano-Sasanian rule and later rulers using Kushan names are not automatically the same state.

profiles.title: Rashtrakuta Empire
profiles.summary: Rashtrakuta imperial power emerged in the Deccan when Dantidurga defeated his Chalukya overlords in the mid-eighth century. Rulers subsequently intervened far into northern India, but successful expeditions did not necessarily create permanent provincial control. The emperor’s authority depended heavily on subordinate rulers, who retained substantial autonomy and their own chains of dependants. Manyakheta became a major court centre, and Amoghavarsha I’s long ninth-century reign is associated with literary and artistic patronage. The wider region’s monuments, including the Hindu, Buddhist and Jain remains at Ellora, show that political geography and religious geography followed different patterns. Around 973, Tailapa II’s revolt displaced the imperial house and opened the way for the later Chalukyas. Other subordinate rulers also sought greater independence.
profiles.continuity: Rashtrakuta is treated here as the imperial Deccan phase, not every family or local ruler bearing the name. Raids toward distant centres should not be read as lasting annexations. Court replacement reorganized existing relationships rather than emptying the region of people.

profiles.title: Srivijaya · maritime court and networks
profiles.summary: Srivijaya emerged around Palembang in southeastern Sumatra in the late seventh century. Its importance rested on river access, maritime exchange and relationships with other ports and rulers, rather than a continuous land frontier. Inscriptions, Buddhist connections and imported objects provide different kinds of evidence for its reach. Chola naval attacks in 1025 disrupted important centres, but the event cannot by itself prove the immediate disappearance of all Srivijayan political or commercial activity. Scholarship has debated whether references across later centuries describe one continuous centralized empire, successive courts, or a changing network. More recent archaeological work supports the long importance of the Palembang region. The broad endpoint around 1400 marks the later medieval transformation of these networks, rather than a securely dated final day.
profiles.continuity: The title retains the atlas name, but empire is not a claim of uniform administration over every coloured island. Both continuity and the relationship between Palembang, Java and the peninsula are research questions. The dates are approximate evidence bounds.

profiles.title: Sukhothai kingdom
profiles.summary: Sukhothai developed as a regional kingdom in the thirteenth century, conventionally beginning in 1238. Its capital and the associated centres of Si Satchanalai and Kamphaeng Phet formed a connected political and economic landscape. Reservoirs, dams, canals and moats linked cultivation, daily water supply, communication and defence. Buddhist monasteries and royal patronage shaped the surviving urban monuments, while ceramic production connected the towns to wider exchange. Inscriptions preserve claims about government, religion and social life, but are voices from particular settings rather than neutral censuses. Sukhothai’s independence diminished as Ayutthaya became dominant. The date 1378 is often used for loss of independent status, while incorporation continued into the fifteenth century; by 1438 the wider kingdom had been absorbed.
profiles.continuity: This profile distinguishes independent kingship from later subordinate continuity. The 1400 atlas observation can refer to a still recognizable Sukhothai political region under Ayutthayan supremacy, not an unchanged sovereign state. The endpoint does not date the end of local settlement or Buddhist practice.

profiles.title: Champa · coastal polities
profiles.summary: Champa denotes a long history of Cham-speaking coastal and river-centred polities in what is now central and southern Vietnam. The conventional starting date of 192 belongs to early state formation; it does not establish a single unchanged kingdom lasting for sixteen centuries. Rulers cultivated Indian-derived religious and political forms while adapting them locally. The temples at Mỹ Sơn preserve especially rich evidence of Shaiva worship, royal patronage, engineering and artistic exchange. Political centres and relationships changed over time. Đại Việt’s invasion of 1471 caused a major rupture, but did not end every Cham principality. Southern centres continued under changing conditions of autonomy and dependence. The last principality was annexed in 1832, an event remembered very differently in Vietnamese administrative records and Cham narratives.
profiles.continuity: A shared label must not collapse several centres, rival rulers and changing tributary relations into one homogeneous state. Cham languages, communities and religious traditions continue beyond the loss of political autonomy. Temple distribution is evidence of patronage, not a population-wide faith map.

profiles.title: Đại Việt · successive kingdoms and divided realms
profiles.summary: Đại Việt was a political name used by several Vietnamese ruling houses, not the name of one dynasty. Adopted in 1054, it linked successive governments centred initially on the Red River region and Thăng Long. The citadel’s archaeological layers show how a durable seat of power could be rebuilt and reinterpreted by different regimes. Court culture developed through local practices and exchange with China and Champa. Over subsequent centuries, dynastic replacement, war and rival political centres altered both the reach and organization of rule. The Hồ period used the name Đại Ngu, followed by Ming occupation; Đại Việt was restored under the Lê in 1428. The name later covered increasingly divided realms before Nguyễn reunification and the adoption of Việt Nam in 1804.
profiles.continuity: Aliases exclude 1400–1427 so that the Hồ name and Ming occupation are not presented as uninterrupted Đại Việt government. The later shared name does not prove that competing courts formed one centrally administered state. Continuity of Thăng Long as a place is distinct from continuity of a ruling house.

profiles.title: Bagan / Pagan kingdom
profiles.summary: Bagan developed from a polity in the central Ayeyarwady basin into a major regional kingdom. Its ninth-century beginnings are much less securely documented than the imperial and monumental phase of the eleventh to thirteenth centuries. Control of river transport helped rulers connect agricultural resources, trading activity and political centres. Kings and other donors accumulated religious merit through monasteries, temples and stupas, making Buddhist patronage an important part of the political economy. Bagan also participated in networks extending beyond the boundaries of any one ruler, including exchanges with Bengal and other Buddhist regions. Royal authority fragmented in the late thirteenth century, conventionally ending the imperial phase around 1287. The sacred landscape and its communities remained active after the capital lost its earlier political role.
profiles.continuity: The 849 opening is a conventional early-polity date, while 1287 is an approximate endpoint for imperial Bagan. Later atlas labels Pagan at 1300 or 1400 are not automatically evidence that this earlier kingdom survived unchanged. Religious continuity substantially outlasted political predominance.

profiles.title: Yamato court · Kofun and Asuka phases
profiles.summary: The Yamato court developed through alliances and competition among regional elites in the Japanese archipelago. Monumental burial mounds and their furnishings reveal concentrated resources and hierarchy, but do not by themselves provide exact political boundaries. By the late fifth century, the Yamato ruling group had secured a dominant position across substantial parts of Honshū and northern Kyūshū. Korean and Chinese contacts carried technologies, writing, religious ideas and people into this evolving order. Buddhism gained influential court patrons during the sixth and seventh centuries, alongside existing ritual traditions. Reforms and written law codes sought to strengthen royal administration, while court seats moved among several locations in the Asuka region. The move to Nara in 710 closes this study phase, rather than marking the extinction of the imperial institution.
profiles.continuity: Yamato can mean a region, a court or an archaeological-historical phase. The alias is therefore bounded to the early court period. The atlas label at 900 is outside this profile and belongs to a later imperial setting, already treated by the Heian history.

profiles.title: Joseon kingdom
profiles.summary: Joseon replaced Goryeo in 1392 and made Neo-Confucian ideas central to court government and elite education. Officials were recruited through examinations within a strongly unequal society in which influential families held enduring advantages. Restrictions on Buddhist institutions changed patterns of patronage, although Buddhism and other practices continued. Embassies to Ming China combined diplomatic hierarchy with trade and cultural exchange; tributary language did not mean ordinary provincial administration by China. Japanese invasions in the late sixteenth century devastated the peninsula, and later defensive works such as Namhansanseong illustrate continued adaptation to regional threats. The court and its institutions persisted through changing internal and foreign pressures. In 1897, Gojong proclaimed the Korean Empire, transforming the state’s title and political programme while continuing the ruling house.
profiles.continuity: Joseon’s kingdom phase ends here at the year before the imperial proclamation to keep annual name matching unambiguous. Art-historical labels often extend the Joseon dynasty to 1910 because the royal lineage continued. This is a change of state form, not a new population.

profiles.title: Korean Empire
profiles.summary: Gojong proclaimed the Korean Empire in October 1897 as part of an effort to defend sovereignty and revise the inherited Joseon political order. The imperial title asserted an independent standing amid competition by foreign powers, while reforms pursued changes in administration and modernization. The continued royal house and much of the existing society connected this short period to the much longer Joseon history. Japanese power expanded sharply during and after the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905. Japan took control of Korea’s foreign affairs, leaving the imperial court with severely restricted authority. In 1910, forced annexation abolished the empire’s sovereignty and inaugurated Japanese colonial rule. The period therefore contains a major change in effective authority before the formal disappearance of the state.
profiles.continuity: A coloured Korea in 1900 belongs to this imperial phase, not the earlier kingdom. The 1905 loss of control over foreign relations must be distinguished from annexation in 1910. Dynastic continuity did not mean unchanged sovereignty.

profiles.title: Ghana / Wagadou
profiles.periodLabel: Gradual formation by the first millennium–c. 1240 CE
profiles.summary: Ghana, known in Soninke traditions as Wagadou, developed south of the Sahara in lands now divided between Mauritania and Mali. Its beginnings cannot be reduced to a securely documented founding year. Agriculture and regional exchange supported communities before royal power grew around the movement of gold, salt and other goods. The court benefited from its position between gold-producing districts and desert trading networks, without necessarily administering the goldfields themselves. Muslim merchants connected the kingdom to North Africa; commercial Islam and royal religious practices coexisted rather than changing everywhere at once. Arabic accounts, including al-Bakri's compilation from travelers' information, describe royal authority and distinct urban communities, while archaeology supplies an independent record of settlement. Identifying every described capital with excavated Kumbi Saleh remains problematic. From the eleventh through thirteenth centuries, competing powers and changing trade connections weakened the kingdom. Sosso and then Mali gained ascendancy in its former sphere. This was a prolonged political reconfiguration, not the disappearance of Soninke society or a proven single-day destruction of an empire.
profiles.continuity: The early date marks a broad formation horizon. Medieval Ghana was geographically distinct from the modern Republic of Ghana. The end around 1240 is an approximate absorption horizon, not a securely dated extinction of its communities.

profiles.title: Kanem–Bornu
profiles.summary: Kanem emerged east of Lake Chad from a region of mobile pastoralists, farmers and trading communities. Its formation is usually placed around the eighth or ninth century, rather than assigned a certain foundation date. Dynastic rulers drew revenue and strategic advantage from routes linking the Lake Chad basin to the Sahara, North Africa and the Nile world. Adoption of Islam by the ruling court in the eleventh century strengthened scholarly and diplomatic connections, while the population retained varied religious practices. In the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries the political center shifted westward toward Bornu. Conflict with the Bulala and dynastic struggles helped drive this relocation; it did not create an unrelated people or sever every older claim. Bornu later recovered influence east of the lake, and the combined historical name Kanem–Bornu expresses this changing center of power. Its widest influence came in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Warfare, tribute and caravan connections produced uneven authority over a large hinterland. The conquest of Bornu in 1893 ended this phase, before European colonial partition divided the region.
profiles.continuity: Kanem and Bornu describe connected but changing centers and dynastic regimes. An imperial outline should not imply equally direct administration across desert dependencies. The 1893 endpoint precedes colonial partition and does not end local political or religious institutions.

profiles.title: Kingdom of Kongo
profiles.summary: Kongo developed around Mbanza Kongo in the late fourteenth century through alliances, marriages and conquest among Kikongo-speaking communities. The capital coordinated provinces and tributary relationships, but the kingdom was not administered uniformly across every territory attributed to it. Contact with Portugal in the 1480s opened sustained Atlantic diplomacy and commerce. Christianity became a language of royal authority, scholarship and local religious creativity, rather than simply replacing all earlier beliefs. Kongolese rulers and elites corresponded with European courts and church authorities while attempting to control foreign merchants. The expanding Atlantic slave trade, struggles over succession and relations with neighboring powers increasingly threatened that control. The death of King António I at Mbwila in 1665 precipitated prolonged factional warfare. Later efforts to restore the kingdom included the religious movement associated with Dona Beatriz Kimpa Vita and renewed occupation of the capital. Royal institutions continued despite diminished and contested power. Portuguese domination intensified in the nineteenth century, and the remaining monarchy was incorporated into colonial Angola in the early twentieth century. Its cultural and religious communities survived these political ruptures.
profiles.continuity: The atlas label Congo is matched only before colonial partition; the Congo Free State and the modern Congolese republics are different entities. The broad dynastic lifespan must not be mistaken for uninterrupted sovereignty or constant borders.

profiles.title: Asante kingdom and empire
profiles.summary: Asante grew from the Akan political landscape of the Gold Coast interior around the beginning of the eighteenth century. Under Osei Tutu, neighboring states were brought into an expanding union centered on Kumasi. Its rulers promoted a shared political identity through existing Akan traditions, court ceremony and the arts, while retaining a hierarchy of constituent authorities. Gold, textiles and participation in the trade in enslaved people contributed to its wealth and military power. By the mid-eighteenth century Asante had become a major regional empire, whose tributary reach should be distinguished from the core governed through Kumasi. Court regalia encoded political relationships and proverbs; they were instruments of government and memory as well as precious objects. Nineteenth-century conflict with Britain and coastal powers repeatedly changed the kingdom’s position. British forces invaded and looted Kumasi in 1874, and further intervention culminated in conquest and annexation around 1900–1901. These events ended independent imperial government but did not extinguish Asante identity or kingship. Dispersed royal objects remain evidence both of earlier statecraft and of the violence of colonial acquisition.
profiles.continuity: This profile covers the independent imperial phase. The Asante royal institution continued under changed political conditions; its survival does not extend the independent empire’s borders into modern Ghana.

profiles.title: Kingdom of Dahomey
profiles.periodLabel: c. 1625–1894 CE; royal succession continued under colonial rule
profiles.summary: Dahomey developed around Abomey during the seventeenth century, consolidating authority over neighboring communities in what is now southern Benin. Its palaces served simultaneously as royal residences, places of administration, ritual centers and repositories of dynastic memory. Successive rulers expanded the complex, while reliefs, objects and oral traditions recorded royal achievements and claims. Expansion toward the coast brought the kingdom into direct contact with Atlantic merchants. The conquest of Ouidah in 1727 provided access to a major port in the trade in enslaved Africans, making warfare, captivity and overseas commerce central to state power. Dahomey’s independence was constrained at times by tribute to the larger Oyo empire; these relationships changed as Oyo weakened. Court organization and military mobilization supported continued nineteenth-century power, even as the Atlantic commercial environment shifted. French campaigns from 1890 to 1894 defeated the monarchy’s resistance and established colonial domination. The removal of royal objects during conquest is part of the surviving evidence’s history. Abomey’s palaces preserve a dynastic tradition extending beyond the loss of political independence, not proof that independent sovereignty lasted unchanged until 1900.
profiles.continuity: The kingdom of Dahomey, the French colony named Dahomey and the postcolonial republic are distinct political phases. UNESCO’s palace chronology follows royal succession through 1900; this profile ends independent rule in 1894.

profiles.title: Old Oyo kingdom and empire
profiles.summary: Oyo developed as a Yoruba kingdom whose traditions linked its rulers to Ife and the ancestral figure Oranmiyan. Such genealogies express political legitimacy and should not be read as a securely dated sequence of early reigns. Its position in the savanna favored horse cavalry and overland connections with northern trading states. Forest ecology and disease limited the same cavalry farther south, helping explain why imperial influence and direct occupation differed. After disruption by Nupe forces in the sixteenth century, Oyo recovered and expanded during the seventeenth. The alaafin ruled within a political system that included powerful council and military offices; authority was negotiated as well as imposed. Tributary relations extended toward the coast, and victory over Dahomey in the late 1720s strengthened access to Atlantic commerce. The export and domestic exploitation of enslaved people were important to its economy. Succession struggles, resistance by dependent states and the rise of Ilorin weakened the empire in the early nineteenth century. Old Oyo was abandoned amid the crises of the 1830s. Later Oyo kingship endured at a different center, within a fragmented and increasingly colonial political landscape.
profiles.continuity: The alias stops with Old Oyo’s imperial collapse. Nineteenth-century observations labeled Oyo may refer to the successor kingdom at New Oyo and should not automatically inherit the former empire’s territorial reach.

profiles.title: Luba kingdoms and imperial network
profiles.summary: Luba political traditions developed across the lake and river country of southeastern Central Africa, with early chronology preserved in narratives of sacred founders rather than contemporary dated annals. During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, royal institutions and networks of allegiance expanded among communities that did not all share identical languages or customs. Sacred kingship worked alongside councils, local leaders and specialists responsible for historical memory. Objects such as royal vessels, staffs and seats helped communicate the legitimacy of rulers and the continuing presence of ancestors. Women were central to this spiritual account of authority, including representations associated with the continuity of kingship. Luba influence therefore cannot be mapped simply as a uniform block of centrally administered territory: shared political forms and artistic practices could spread beyond effective royal command. The eighteenth century brought an increasingly imperial network, while nineteenth-century commerce changed its balance. Expanding trades in ivory and enslaved people strengthened competing military entrepreneurs and undermined established rulers. In the late nineteenth century the larger imperial sphere fragmented amid violence, before and during European colonial expansion. Luba communities and institutions continued under new political constraints.
profiles.continuity: Luba names a connected set of political and cultural traditions, not one permanently centralized nation-state. The displayed dates bound the principal imperial phase; neither endpoint is an attested single founding or dissolution day.

profiles.title: Lunda empire and commonwealth
profiles.summary: Lunda developed south of the Luba heartland through the consolidation of chiefly authority and an adaptable system of political affiliation. Traditions associate its foundation with the arrival of Chibinda Ilunga, a hunter connected to Luba, and his marriage into a local ruling family around 1600. This is an origin narrative, not a contemporary register establishing an exact foundation. Lunda rulers adopted elements of neighboring statecraft while retaining an independent political center. By the mid-seventeenth century, royal initiatives linked the interior to Atlantic trading connections; other branches subsequently connected copper districts and routes toward eastern Africa. Expansion created related courts and dependent authorities across a wide area, often better understood as a commonwealth of relationships than a single homogeneous administration. Wealth from tribute and commerce supported elaborate insignia and the circulation of courtly art. During the nineteenth century, the same wider commercial world strengthened Chokwe traders and other regional competitors. Ivory and slave trading, armed entrepreneurs and local struggles progressively eroded the central rulers’ control. By the closing decades of the century the imperial network was breaking into competing chiefdoms, followed by colonial partition. Related Lunda authorities and identities outlasted that transformation.
profiles.continuity: Luba ancestry in Lunda traditions does not make Lunda a continuously subordinate Luba province. The c. 1890 endpoint summarizes late nineteenth-century fragmentation, not an instantaneous disappearance of all related courts.

profiles.title: Kuba kingdom
profiles.summary: The Kuba kingdom brought together several principalities in the forest and savanna between the Kasai, Sankuru and Lulua rivers. Oral history credits Shyaam aMbul aNgoong with unification around 1625 and associates his innovations with knowledge gained through travel to western neighbors. The dating and personal details belong to a remembered foundation, not a surviving contemporary chronicle. Agricultural change, ironworking and a system of ranked offices supported a wealthy court while distributing responsibilities among titled authorities. Kuba artists developed textiles, containers, costume and sculpture that made social standing visible. Royal ndop figures, associated with a tradition established around 1700, preserved idealized images of kings and their identifying emblems. These objects were historical instruments as well as works of art. Nineteenth-century trade increased access to wealth, but European colonial expansion eventually imposed a new political framework. Museum provenance research places the removal of court objects in the context of military pressure during the early twentieth century, complicating older descriptions of voluntary gifts. The loss of independent power did not erase the royal institution or the communities that maintained Kuba artistic and historical knowledge.
profiles.continuity: The approximate endpoint marks the early twentieth-century colonial transition, not the death of Kuba kingship. Colonial sovereignty claims beginning in 1885 must not be confused with immediate control on the ground.

profiles.title: Mutapa / Mwenemutapa
profiles.periodLabel: c. mid-15th century–1902 CE; successive reduced regimes
profiles.summary: Mutapa emerged in the northern Zimbabwean plateau and Zambezi region during the fifteenth century. Traditions connect its founders with the wider political world associated with Great Zimbabwe, but a simple mass migration from one capital to another is not established. Farming, cattle, gold and ivory supported rulers whose authority depended on tribute and relationships with regional chiefs. Muslim commercial networks connected the interior with the Indian Ocean; Portuguese merchants and officials increasingly entered these circuits during the sixteenth century. Their written accounts are valuable but often exaggerate the size and resources of the realm. Succession disputes and interference by outside forces weakened royal control. In 1629, a Portuguese-supported claimant accepted a treaty of subordination, yet this did not instantly convert every community into a directly governed Portuguese colony. Later Mutapa rulers retained varying degrees of autonomy as the Rozvi and regional landholders expanded. The monarchy survived in a much reduced Zambezi political landscape through the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Renewed resistance to Portuguese expansion around the turn of the twentieth century ended with the death of Chioko in 1902, the conventional endpoint adopted here.
profiles.continuity: Distinguish the earlier tributary sphere, seventeenth-century treaties and later reduced dynastic regimes. Mutapa was not identical to Great Zimbabwe, and its later survival does not justify retaining its maximum territorial outline.

profiles.title: Sokoto Caliphate
profiles.summary: The Sokoto Caliphate arose from the religious reform movement and war led by Usman dan Fodio from 1804. Victories over Hausa rulers created a new political order whose authority was justified through Islamic scholarship, law and the claimed obligations of just government. It was a federation of emirates with substantial local administration, not a territory governed identically from one capital. Leadership was divided between western and eastern centers, and Muhammad Bello consolidated the Sokoto-centered regime after his father’s death in 1817. Scholarship and agricultural expansion accompanied commerce across the savanna, but the economy also relied heavily on enslavement, slave raiding and coerced agricultural labor. Understanding the caliphate requires considering those subjected to its power alongside the writings of its reforming elites. Nineteenth-century rulers faced recurrent revolts and uneven control over distant emirates. British commercial and military encroachment intensified toward the century’s end. The capture of Sokoto and the defeat of the last resisting caliph in 1903 ended independent political rule. Colonial authorities retained and reshaped emirate institutions, while the Sokoto title continued as a religious authority under a fundamentally different sovereign framework.
profiles.continuity: Fulani Empire is an older atlas label for a diverse Islamic polity; it should not imply one homogeneous ethnic population. The post-1903 sultanate and emirates continued under colonial rule, without the former caliphate’s independent sovereignty.

profiles.title: Merina monarchy / Kingdom of Madagascar
profiles.summary: The Merina monarchy grew from a landscape of fortified communities and competing royal centers in Madagascar’s central highlands. Its earlier history cannot be mapped as an already unified island kingdom. Ambohimanga preserves evidence of this developing political culture: defensive gateways, royal compounds, places of judgment, ancestor worship and agricultural land were parts of one system of authority. During the eighteenth century, consolidation around the hill strengthened a dynasty that later united the highland realm and expanded its ambitions across Madagascar. The principal royal residence moved to Antananarivo before the end of that century, while Ambohimanga retained exceptional religious and funerary importance. International recognition from 1817 marked a new phase of the kingdom’s external relations, not the beginning of Malagasy society. Nineteenth-century architecture and court spaces show changing relationships with European powers alongside continuing local institutions. French annexation in 1896 and the dismantling of royal authority transformed this political landscape. In 1897 the colonial administration removed royal remains from Ambohimanga and established its own presence. The dynasty lost state power, but the sacred landscape remained a focus of worship and historical memory.
profiles.continuity: The opening date is a broad highland formation horizon. Merina political expansion did not make all Malagasy peoples identical. The move of the royal residence did not end Ambohimanga’s role as a sacred capital.

profiles.title: Empire of Brazil
profiles.summary: Brazil’s imperial state emerged from independence from Portugal in 1822, with a monarchy that retained connections to the Portuguese royal house. The constitution of 1824 established a representative system combining an emperor, a senate and a chamber of deputies, within a highly unequal society. Independence did not abolish slavery. Pedro I’s abdication in 1831 left the country governed by regents during his son’s minority, a period marked by conflicts over authority and regional unrest. Declaring Pedro II of age in 1840 brought a new phase of imperial government. Parliamentary institutions, ministers and the crown shared an evolving political system whose stability rested in part on restrictive social and electoral arrangements. Brazil’s participation with Argentina and Uruguay in the war against Paraguay from 1864 to 1870 enlarged the political importance of the army. Debate and campaigning against slavery culminated in its legal abolition in 1888. Conflict among the monarchy, military and influential political and economic groups intensified. In November 1889 military action displaced the imperial government and established a republic. The state continued, but its constitutional and dynastic form changed decisively.

profiles.title: Haiti
profiles.summary: Haiti became independent in 1804 after the revolution that began with the 1791 uprising of enslaved people in French Saint-Domingue. The struggle passed through civil war, foreign intervention, the abolition of slavery and renewed French attempts to impose control. Independence made emancipation central to the new state, but did not resolve conflict over land, labor or political authority. After an early division between northern and southern regimes, reunification in 1820 preceded Haitian rule over the eastern part of Hispaniola until 1844. France’s recognition in 1825 was tied to an indemnity that imposed a lasting financial burden. Recurrent internal struggles and foreign pressures shaped the nineteenth century. United States occupation from 1915 to 1934 reorganized government while severely constraining Haitian sovereignty. The Duvalier family dictatorship lasted from 1957 to 1986; subsequent efforts to establish democratic government faced coups, international intervention and profound social inequality. The state endured through these changes of regime. By the beginning of 2025, United Nations reporting described a transitional political process amid armed-group violence and a severe humanitarian crisis. That dated assessment is an endpoint for this account, not a prediction about Haiti’s future.
profiles.continuity: The independent state begins in 1804; an atlas label Haiti in 1715 describes a place or colonial context and must not inherit this profile. The 2025 endpoint denotes research coverage, not dissolution.

profiles.title: Viceroyalty of New Spain
profiles.summary: New Spain developed from the conquest of Mexico-Tenochtitlan and its allies, but the viceroyalty itself was formally established in 1535. Earlier military and judicial offices had already begun building colonial government. From Mexico City, overlapping viceregal, judicial and ecclesiastical institutions governed an expanding and internally diverse set of territories. Local Indigenous communities remained important political actors, although conquest, tribute obligations and religious coercion fundamentally changed the conditions under which they acted. Surviving tribute records, land claims, genealogies and books reveal negotiation and resistance alongside exploitation. The viceroy’s correspondence connects Mexico with other Spanish possessions, including the Philippines, and demonstrates why a simple contiguous map cannot capture the jurisdiction’s wider reach. The eighteenth-century Bourbon monarchy attempted to centralize administration and revenue, aggravating conflicts over privilege and access to office. The crisis of Spanish monarchy during the Napoleonic period and the insurgency beginning in 1810 produced a prolonged struggle over legitimate government. In 1821 the colonial regime in Mexico gave way to an independent empire. Former dependencies followed different political paths, so the viceroyalty’s disappearance should not be treated as a simultaneous national founding everywhere it once claimed authority.

profiles.title: Viceroyalty of Peru
profiles.summary: The Spanish crown created the Viceroyalty of Peru in 1542, following the invasion of the Inka realm and a decade of conflict. Lima became the principal center of royal administration, while older Andean centers and local communities remained essential to the functioning and contestation of colonial rule. The jurisdiction initially claimed a vast part of Spanish South America, with authority exercised through different institutions and regional intermediaries. Silver mining made the viceroyalty central to global commerce. Potosí’s mines, mills and mint depended in part on forced Indigenous labor under the colonial mita, linking American extraction with imperial finance and distant markets. Universities, churches and printing helped circulate official knowledge, while Indigenous and mixed-ancestry authors also recorded critiques and alternative histories. Eighteenth-century creation of New Granada and Río de la Plata removed major territories from Lima’s jurisdiction. Independence was another extended and uneven process: the declaration in Lima in 1821 did not eliminate royalist government in the highlands. The defeat of the viceroy’s army at Ayacucho in 1824 ended the principal viceregal regime. Colonial social institutions and regional inequalities did not vanish with that military settlement.
profiles.continuity: The viceroyalty was larger than modern Peru and changed jurisdiction repeatedly. Lima’s independence declaration and the final defeat of the main royalist army mark different stages; local Spanish holdouts survived beyond 1824.

profiles.title: Tuʻi Tonga polity and maritime network
profiles.summary: The Tuʻi Tonga polity developed from older island communities into a stratified political network whose archaeological state formation is generally placed around 1200–1300. Monumental centers at Heketa and later Lapaha show the mobilization of labor and the material expression of chiefly authority. Stone buildings, tombs and imported tools offer evidence independent of later genealogical accounts, although their dating often spans decades or centuries. Geochemical analysis of stone tools documents connections between Tonga, Fiji, Samoa and other islands. These finds show sustained movement of people and valuable materials; they do not by themselves prove that every source island was a directly ruled province. Chiefs used descent, marriage, ceremony and exchange to build relationships across a maritime world. Tribute and ritual gatherings helped connect local production with elite centers, while authority changed among chiefly lines over time. In the late eighteenth century, escalating conflict undermined the older order. Archaeological studies use 1799 as a major transition into prolonged warfare that reshaped the islands before nineteenth-century reunification under a new monarchy. Communities and chiefly traditions continued through this rupture, making it a transformation of power rather than the end of Tongan history.
profiles.continuity: The atlas’s Empire label exceeds what imported artifacts alone can demonstrate. This profile begins with the better-supported archaeological state horizon; earlier genealogical dates and the warfare after 1799 are not silently assigned the same political structure.

profiles.title: Kingdom of Tonga
profiles.summary: The modern Kingdom of Tonga emerged from nineteenth-century reunification under George Tupou I in 1845, after a prolonged period of rivalry and warfare among chiefly powers. This consolidation drew on older Tongan institutions while establishing a new dynastic and constitutional framework. The constitution of 1875 set out a monarchy with representative institutions, giving the modern state a legal foundation distinct from the earlier maritime networks associated with the Tuʻi Tonga. Under the relationship established with Britain in 1900, Tonga retained its monarchy while British protection constrained external sovereignty. The arrangement ended in 1970, when Tonga assumed full responsibility for its international affairs and joined the Commonwealth. Subsequent constitutional debates concerned how authority should be distributed among monarch, nobles and elected representatives. Reforms culminating in the 2010 election made the Legislative Assembly responsible for choosing the prime minister and strengthened its role in holding the executive accountable. Royal and noble institutions continued alongside these changes. The kingdom therefore illustrates political continuity through major changes in sovereignty and representation, rather than an unchanged form of government extending back to the medieval Pacific. This account’s modern endpoint is 2025.
